page: The Vultr vhf-4c-16gb is an instance within the High Frequency Compute series configured with 4 shared vCPUs mapped to 2 physical cores on an Intel x86_64 architecture operating at 2.0 GHz. The system provides 16.0 GB of system memory, matching a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio at 4.0 GB per vCPU. Hardware resources also include 384 GB of local NVMe SSD storage and a single complimentary public IPv4 address, with no hardware GPU acceleration provisioned.

Benchmark results demonstrate balanced mid-tier compute capabilities alongside certain I/O limitations. General compute execution aligns with the median tier, evidenced by a Geekbench multi-core score of 4781.0, single-core score of 1625.0, and a PassMark CPU score of 7697.28. Synthetic compiler and algorithmic benchmarks reflect stable mid-range performance, such as 7042.0 in Clang compilation and 6644.0 in ray tracing. Cached memory bandwidth reaches 497.33 GB/sec in small 16 KB blocks.

Performance constraints emerge in heavy memory throughput and specific scale-intensive workloads. Uncached large-block read operations drop to 35.47 GB/sec, while write operations reach 17.49 GB/sec. Data processing tasks like single-threaded gzip compression at 22.91 GB/sec and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression at 23.47 GB/sec sit in lower benchmark percentiles. Similarly, I/O-sensitive operations such as Redis SET (6.0 million operations/sec), PassMark database operations (2003.37), and static web serving (5.46 GB/sec) trail higher-tier architectures.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the shared-vCPU model provides a practical entry point for balanced multi-threaded tasks that do not require dedicated core tenancy. The inclusion of bundled 384 GB NVMe storage offers local density without attached block storage overhead. The configuration functions best for standard application hosting, development environments, CI/CD runners, and staging workloads where occasional shared-thread contention does not impact operational requirements.

Benchmarking reflects consistent mid-tier performance across general processing, recording 4781.0 in Geekbench multi-core and 7697.28 in PassMark CPU tests. While small-block cached memory bandwidth is robust at 497.33 GB/sec, large uncached read and write bandwidths measure lower at 35.47 GB/sec and 17.49 GB/sec. Consequently, throughput-heavy tasks such as high-volume Redis operations, large-scale compression, and high-concurrency static web serving show measurable baseline constraints. This hardware footprint is suitable for general-purpose application workloads, software builds, and development servers requiring local NVMe storage.
